Anderson Squat: Set the safety pins at the bottom of your squat and start each rep from dead stop with no bounce. Brace hard, drive up through the whole foot, then lower back onto the pins under control. Most people rest too long between reps and lose the tension they built.
Arnold Press: Start with dumbbells at shoulder height and palms facing you, elbows low. Press up while rotating your palms forward, finishing overhead, then reverse the turn on the way down. Rushing the rotation turns it into a normal press and loses the point of the exercise.
B-Stance Hip Thrust: Sit against a bench with the bar over your hips, one foot flat and the other resting lightly on its toes just ahead. Drive through the flat heel to lift your hips, squeezing the glute on that side at the top. Letting the back foot do the work defeats the single-leg bias.
B-Stance Romanian Deadlift: Stand with the bar at your thighs, one foot forward taking most of the weight and the other staggered back on its toes for balance. Push your hips back and lower the bar down your legs, then drive the hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back is the usual fault as the bar passes the knee.
Barbell Back Squat: Set the bar across your upper back, brace your core and unrack it, then step back and set your stance. Bend the hips and knees together to sit down and back, then drive up through the middle of your foot. Letting the knees cave inwards on the way up is the most common breakdown.
Barbell Bench Press: Lie back with your feet planted and the bar over your eyes. Lower the bar to the lower chest with your elbows tucked slightly, then press it back over your shoulders. Let the bar drift towards your neck and the press gets harder, so keep the touch point low.
Barbell Curl: Stand tall holding the bar with an underhand grip and elbows pinned to your sides. Curl the bar up by bending the elbow alone, then lower it back under control. Swinging the hips to sling the bar up takes the work off the biceps.
Barbell Drag Curl: Hold the bar at your thighs with an underhand grip and stand tall. Drag the bar straight up your body, letting the elbows travel back rather than forward, then lower it the same path. Letting the bar swing away from your torso turns it into a regular curl.
Barbell Front Raise: Hold the bar in front of your thighs with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Keeping the elbows softly locked, raise the bar in front of you to around shoulder height, then lower it under control. Using momentum from the lower back to heave the bar up is the common shortcut.
Barbell Front Squat: Rest the bar across the front of your shoulders with your elbows lifted high and upper arms close to parallel with the floor. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. Letting the elbows drop pitches you forward and dumps the bar.
Barbell Good Morning: Set the bar across your upper back as you would for a squat and stand with a soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower your torso towards horizontal, keeping the bar over your feet, then drive the hips forward to stand tall. Rounding through the back instead of hinging is the main fault to avoid.
Barbell Hip Thrust: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench and the bar rolled over your hips. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, then lower under control. Overextending the lower back at the top is the usual mistake.
Barbell Lunge: Stand tall with the bar across your upper back and take a controlled step forward. Lower your back knee towards the floor while keeping your front shin close to vertical, then push back to standing. Letting the front knee drift far past the toes over-loads the knee joint.
Barbell Overhead Press: Stand with the bar resting on your front shoulders, grip just outside shoulder width. Press the bar straight up, moving your head back slightly to let it pass, then guide it back down to the shoulders. Pressing the bar forward instead of straight up wastes effort and stalls the lockout.
Barbell Row (Bent Over): Hinge forward from the hips with a flat back and let the bar hang under your shoulders. Pull the bar up towards your lower ribs, driving the elbows back, then lower it under control. Standing up out of the hinge as you pull turns the row into a shrug.
Barbell Row (Supinated): Hinge forward with a flat back and take an underhand grip on the bar just outside your hips. Pull the bar to your lower ribs by driving your elbows back and down, then lower it with control. Letting the torso rise as you pull shortens the range and shifts the load off the back.
Barbell Shrug: Stand tall holding the bar at arm's length in front of your thighs. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause briefly, then lower them fully. Rolling the shoulders in a circle adds nothing and just wastes the tension.
Barbell Skull Crusher: Lie on a bench holding the bar over your chest with a shoulder-width grip. Bend your elbows to lower the bar towards your forehead, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back to the start. Letting the elbows flare or drift back turns the move into a different press.
Barbell Upright Row (Wide): Hold the bar with a wide overhand grip in front of your thighs. Pull the bar straight up towards your collarbone, leading with your elbows out to the sides, then lower with control. Using a narrow grip on this version pulls the stress into the wrists and shoulders.
Barbell Wrist Curl: Sit and rest your forearms on your thighs with your wrists just past your knees, palms up, holding the bar. Curl your wrists up as far as they will comfortably go, then lower until the bar rolls to your fingertips. Using the whole forearm to swing the bar defeats the point of the isolation.
Batwing Row: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down. Row both dumbbells up, driving your elbows back and pinching your shoulder blades together, then lower fully. Letting the chest lift off the bench brings the lower back into the lift.
Behind-the-Back Barbell Shrug: Stand tall holding the bar behind you at arm's length, resting against your glutes. Shrug your shoulders straight up towards your ears, then lower them fully. This grip needs a shorter bar path than the front version, so avoid trying to shrug as high.
Behind-the-Back Wrist Curl (Barbell): Stand tall holding the bar behind your hips with an overhand grip. Curl your wrists upward, letting the bar roll towards your fingers first, then reverse to extend the wrists back down. Moving the shoulders or elbows to help the lift takes the work off the forearms.
Bench Press (Close Grip, Dumbbell): Lie on a bench holding two dumbbells together over your chest with palms facing each other. Lower the dumbbells to the sides of your chest keeping your elbows tucked, then press them back up and together. Letting the dumbbells drift apart on the way down turns it into a regular press.
Board Press: Lie on a bench with a block or boards resting on your chest and the bar held above. Lower the bar until it touches the board, pause briefly, then press back up. Bouncing the bar off the board instead of pausing removes the point of the drill.
Box Squat: Set a box or bench at your target squat depth and stand in front of it with the bar on your back. Sit back onto the box under control, pause without relaxing, then drive back up. Collapsing down onto the box instead of controlling the descent jars the lower back.
Bradford Press: Stand holding the bar at shoulder height in front of your face. Press it just above your head and lower it behind your neck to shoulder height, then press it back up and return it to the front. Pressing the bar too high defeats the short, controlled path this move relies on.
Bulgarian Split Squat: Stand a stride's length in front of a bench and rest the top of your back foot on it, holding dumbbells at your sides. Lower your back knee towards the floor by bending the front leg, then push back up through the front foot. Letting the front knee cave inward under fatigue is the main thing to watch.
Cambered Bar Squat: Set the curved bar across your upper back, noting the load hangs lower and swings slightly more than a straight bar. Squat down keeping your torso upright and knees tracking your toes, then drive back up. Fighting the natural sway of the bar rather than staying braced makes the lift feel unstable.
Chest-Supported Row (Barbell): Lie face down on an inclined bench with the bar held underneath you, arms hanging straight. Row the bar up to your torso by driving your elbows back, then lower it fully under control. Lifting your chest off the pad to cheat the pull removes the support the exercise is built around.
Chest-Supported Row (Dumbbell): Lie face down on an inclined bench holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down. Row both dumbbells up towards your ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then lower fully. Shrugging the shoulders up towards the ears instead of pulling with the back is the common fault.
Chest-Supported T-Bar Row: Lie chest-down on the pad with your arms hanging straight down to the handles. Row the handles up towards your torso, leading with your elbows, then lower under full control. Yanking the weight with a jerk instead of a smooth pull shortens the range you actually use.
Clean Pull: Stand over the bar with your shins close to it and hips higher than in a deadlift. Drive through the floor to pull the bar up your legs, finishing tall with your shoulders shrugged, without trying to catch it. Bending the elbows early turns the pull into a poor row instead of a clean extension.
Close-Grip Bench Press: Lie on the bench and take a grip just inside shoulder width on the bar. Lower it to your lower chest keeping your elbows tucked close to your sides, then press back up. Letting the elbows flare wide turns this into a normal bench press and takes the focus off the triceps.
Close-Grip Floor Press: Lie on the floor with knees bent and take a close grip on the bar held over your chest. Lower your elbows until your upper arms touch the floor, then press the bar back up. Letting the elbows flare out at the bottom shifts the load away from the triceps.
Concentration Curl: Sit on a bench, lean forward and brace your elbow against the inside of your thigh, dumbbell hanging below. Curl the weight up towards your shoulder, then lower it fully with control. Letting the elbow drift off the thigh turns the exercise into a standing curl.
Conventional Deadlift: Stand with the bar over the middle of your feet, grip just outside your legs, and set your hips down with a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout. Letting the bar drift forward away from your body rounds the lower back under load.
Cross-Body Hammer Curl: Stand holding a dumbbell in one hand with your palm facing your body. Curl the dumbbell up and across towards the opposite shoulder, then lower it back down the same path. Letting the elbow swing away from your side turns this into a swinging motion rather than a curl.
Cuban Press: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides and raise them out and up until your upper arms are level with your shoulders, elbows bent. From there, rotate your forearms up until the dumbbells point overhead, then press to full extension and reverse the whole sequence. Rushing through the rotation phase skips the part the exercise is meant to train.
Curtsy Lunge: Stand tall and step one leg diagonally behind and across the other, lowering into a lunge as your knees bend. Push back through the front leg to return to standing, then repeat or switch sides. Letting the front knee twist inward as you step across is the main fault.
Curtsy Lunge (Glute Focus): Stand tall and step one leg diagonally behind and across the other, sitting your hips back as you lower. Drive through the front heel to return to standing, keeping the torso slightly forward to load the glute. Rushing back up onto the toes takes the tension off the working glute.
Cyclist Squat: Stand with your heels elevated on plates or a wedge, feet close together, bar on your back. Squat straight down keeping your torso upright and knees tracking forward over your toes, then stand back up. Letting the heels lift further off the wedge changes the exercise and strains the ankles.
Deadlift (Conventional): Stand with the bar over the middle of your feet, grip just outside your legs, and set your hips down with a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout. Letting the bar drift forward away from your body rounds the lower back under load.
Deadlift (Sumo): Stand with a wide stance, toes turned out, gripping the bar inside your knees with a flat back. Push your knees out in the direction of your toes and drive through the floor to stand tall. Letting the hips shoot up faster than the chest turns the pull into a stiff-legged lift.
Decline Barbell Bench Press: Lie on a decline bench with your feet secured and take a shoulder-width grip on the bar. Lower it to your lower chest, then press it back up over your shoulders. Losing the tightness in your feet and hips lets the whole body slide during the press.
Decline Dumbbell Fly: Lie on a decline bench holding dumbbells above your chest with a slight bend in the elbows. Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch across the chest, then bring them back together over your chest. Bending the elbows more as the weight gets heavy turns the fly into a press.
Decline Dumbbell Press: Lie on a decline bench holding dumbbells at chest height with your feet secured. Press the dumbbells up and slightly together, then lower them back to the sides of your chest. Letting the dumbbells drift out wide at the bottom puts unwanted strain on the shoulders.
Decline Skull Crusher: Lie on a decline bench holding the bar over your chest with a shoulder-width grip. Bend your elbows to lower the bar towards your forehead, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back up. Letting the elbows drift wide changes what the exercise is loading.
Deficit Deadlift: Stand on a small platform so the bar starts lower than usual, feet under the bar and hips set with a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the bar close throughout the longer range. Trying to use full deadlift weight straight away often causes the back to round early.
Deficit Reverse Lunge (Glute Focus): Stand on a small platform holding dumbbells, then step one leg back and down off the platform into a lunge. Push through the front heel to return to standing, keeping the torso leaning slightly forward. Rushing the step back reduces the extra range the deficit is there to add.
Dumbbell Bench Press: Lie on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand over your chest, palms facing your feet. Lower the dumbbells to the sides of your chest with elbows at roughly a right angle, then press them back up. Letting the dumbbells drop too low can strain the shoulders, so stop the descent once you feel a stretch.
Dumbbell Calf Raise (Standing): Stand holding dumbbells at your sides with the balls of your feet on a raised edge. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, then lower your heels below the edge for a full stretch. Bouncing at the bottom instead of pausing takes the tension off the calf.
Dumbbell Curl: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with your palms facing forward and elbows at your sides. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then lower them under control. Swinging the shoulders to help the weight up takes the work away from the biceps.
Dumbbell Floor Skull Crusher: Lie on the floor with knees bent, holding dumbbells above your chest with arms extended. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells towards your head, stopping when your upper arms touch the floor, then extend back up. Letting the elbows flare out changes where the tension goes.
Dumbbell Fly: Lie on a bench holding dumbbells above your chest with a slight bend in the elbows. Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch across your chest, then bring them back together above you. Bending the elbows more as the set goes on turns the fly into a press.
Dumbbell Front Raise: Stand holding dumbbells in front of your thighs with palms facing your legs. Raise one or both dumbbells in front of you to around shoulder height, then lower under control. Leaning back to help the weight up shifts the effort onto the lower back.
Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Sit against a bench with a dumbbell resting on your hips and feet flat on the floor. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your body forms a straight line, squeezing your glutes at the top, then lower under control. Pushing through the toes instead of the heels pulls the work into the quads.
Dumbbell Lateral Raise: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides with a slight bend in the elbows. Raise your arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height, then lower under control. Using momentum to swing the weights up past shoulder height takes the tension off the shoulder.
Dumbbell Lunge: Stand tall holding dumbbells at your sides and step forward into a lunge. Lower your back knee towards the floor while your front shin stays close to vertical, then push back to standing. Letting the front knee travel far past the toes puts unnecessary strain on the joint.
Dumbbell Overhead Tricep Extension: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell with both hands behind your head, elbows pointing forward. Extend your arms to press the dumbbell overhead, then lower it back behind your head under control. Letting the elbows flare outward spreads the load away from the triceps.
Dumbbell Pronation/Supination: Sit with your forearm resting on your thigh, holding a dumbbell loaded to one side like a hammer. Rotate your forearm to turn the dumbbell from palm down to palm up and back, keeping the elbow still. Letting the elbow lift off your thigh brings the shoulder into a movement meant for the forearm.
Dumbbell Pullover: Lie across a bench with your head supported and hips low, holding a dumbbell above your chest with both hands. Lower the dumbbell back behind your head in an arc, keeping a slight bend in the elbows, then pull it back over your chest. Letting the hips sag towards the floor takes tension off the target muscles.
Dumbbell Pullover (Chest): Lie across a bench with your head supported and hips low, holding a dumbbell above your chest with both hands. Lower the dumbbell back behind your head in an arc, keeping a slight bend in the elbows, then pull it back over your chest. Letting the hips sag towards the floor takes tension off the target muscles.
Dumbbell Rear Delt Fly: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding dumbbells hanging straight below you. Raise your arms out to the sides, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then lower under control. Bending the elbows heavily turns the fly into a row and shifts the focus to the back.
Dumbbell Row: Rest one knee and hand on a bench, keeping your back flat, and hold a dumbbell in the other hand hanging below your shoulder. Pull the dumbbell up towards your hip, driving your elbow back, then lower it fully. Twisting the torso to help the weight up takes the work away from the back.
Dumbbell Shoulder Press: Sit or stand holding dumbbells at shoulder height with your palms facing forward. Press the dumbbells straight up until your arms are extended, then lower them back to shoulder height. Arching the lower back to help the press up puts strain where the shoulders should be doing the work.
Dumbbell Shrug: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause briefly, then lower them fully. Bending the elbows to help the weight up takes tension off the traps.
Dumbbell Side Bend: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side, the other hand resting on your hip or head. Bend sideways towards the weighted side as far as feels comfortable, then return to upright, keeping the motion in one plane. Twisting the torso as you bend turns it into a different exercise.
Dumbbell Side-Lying Rear Delt: Lie on your side on a bench or the floor, holding a dumbbell above your hip with a slight bend in the elbow. Raise the dumbbell up towards the ceiling, leading with the back of your shoulder, then lower under control. Rolling the torso backward to help the lift takes tension off the rear shoulder.
Dumbbell Single-Leg RDL: Stand on one leg holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand, with a soft bend in the standing knee. Hinge forward at the hip, letting your free leg rise behind you for balance, until your torso is close to horizontal. Rounding the lower back to reach further down is the usual mistake as balance wobbles.
Dumbbell Skull Crusher: Lie on a bench holding dumbbells above your chest with arms extended. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells towards your head, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back up. Letting the elbows drift outward spreads the effort away from the triceps.
Dumbbell Squeeze Press: Lie on a bench holding two dumbbells pressed together over your chest, squeezing them into each other throughout. Lower them to your chest keeping the squeeze on, then press back up without letting them separate. Loosening the inward squeeze partway through removes the whole point of the exercise.
Dumbbell Tibialis Raise (Seated): Sit with your heels on the floor and a dumbbell resting across the top of your feet near the toes. Lift your toes and the front of your feet upward against the weight, then lower under control. Lifting the heels off the floor to help the movement takes the work off the shin muscles.
Dumbbell Wrist Curl: Sit and rest your forearms on your thighs, palms up, holding a dumbbell in each hand. Curl your wrists up as far as comfortable, then lower until the dumbbells roll towards your fingertips. Moving the whole forearm instead of just the wrist reduces the isolation.
Dumbbell Y-Raise: Stand holding light dumbbells and raise your arms up and out to form a Y shape above your head, thumbs leading. Lower them back down under control, keeping a slight bend in the elbows throughout. Using heavier weight than the shoulder can control turns the raise into a shrug.
Egyptian Lateral Raise: Stand side-on to a support, holding it with your free hand and leaning your torso away from the raising arm. Raise the dumbbell out to the side, letting the lean add extra range, then lower under control. Standing upright instead of leaning away removes the extra stretch this version is built for.
EZ Bar Curl: Stand holding the angled bar on its outer grips with your elbows at your sides. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it under control. Letting the elbows drift forward as the weight gets heavy turns the curl into a swinging motion.
EZ Bar Drag Curl: Stand holding the angled bar with your elbows at your sides. Drag the bar up close to your body, letting your elbows travel backward rather than staying still, then lower along the same path. Letting the bar swing away from the torso turns this into a normal curl.
EZ Bar Preacher Curl: Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting on the pad and the bar held with an underhand grip. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it until your arms are almost straight. Lifting your upper arms off the pad to finish the rep takes the strictness out of the movement.
EZ Bar Skull Crusher: Lie on a bench holding the angled bar over your chest with your hands on the angled grips. Bend your elbows to lower the bar towards your forehead, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back up. Letting the elbows flare out spreads the load away from the triceps.
Farmer Walk (Forearms): Stand between two heavy dumbbells or handles, grip them firmly and stand up tall. Walk forward with short controlled steps, keeping your shoulders back and grip locked on. Letting the shoulders round forward under the weight is the usual early sign of losing form.
Farmer's Walk: Stand between two heavy dumbbells or handles, grip them firmly and stand up tall. Walk forward with short controlled steps, keeping your shoulders back and torso upright. Letting the weights swing wildly with each step wastes energy and strains the grip.
Fat Grip Curl: Stand holding a bar fitted with thick grips or wrapped padding, elbows at your sides. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it under control, focusing on keeping a firm grip throughout. Letting the grip loosen partway through the set is the main reason this version feels harder.
Floor Press (Dumbbell): Lie on the floor with knees bent, holding dumbbells above your chest with arms extended. Lower the dumbbells until your upper arms touch the floor, pause briefly, then press back up. Bouncing the elbows off the floor instead of pausing skips the point of the pause.
Front Squat (Dumbbell): Hold dumbbells up at your shoulders, resting against the front of them, elbows lifted. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. Letting the elbows drop lets the dumbbells slide down and pulls you forward.
Goblet Squat: Hold a dumbbell vertically against your chest with both hands cupping the top end. Squat down between your knees keeping your torso upright, then drive back up to standing. Letting the weight pull your torso forward and down is the most common breakdown as depth increases.
Good Morning: Set the bar across your upper back as you would for a squat and stand with a soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower your torso towards horizontal, keeping the bar over your feet, then drive the hips forward to stand tall. Rounding through the back instead of hinging is the main fault to avoid.
Good Morning (Barbell): Set the bar across your upper back as you would for a squat and stand with a soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower your torso towards horizontal, keeping the bar over your feet, then drive the hips forward to stand tall. Rounding through the back instead of hinging is the main fault to avoid.
Gripper Walks: Hold a dumbbell or handle in each hand and squeeze your grip firmly before you start walking. Walk forward with steady steps, keeping your shoulders back and grip locked the whole way. Letting the grip loosen between steps defeats the point of the drill.
Guillotine Press: Lie on a bench and lower the bar to your upper chest or collarbone rather than the usual lower chest spot, elbows flared slightly. Press the bar back up over your shoulders under control. This bar path asks more of the front shoulder, so keep the weight lighter than a standard bench press.
Half-Kneeling Shoulder Press: Kneel on one knee with the other foot planted in front, holding a dumbbell at shoulder height on the same side as the down knee. Press the dumbbell straight overhead, then lower it back to shoulder height. Letting the hips shift sideways to help the press takes the stability challenge out of the exercise.
Hammer Curl: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing your body throughout. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then lower them under control. Rotating the wrists during the curl turns it into a regular curl and misses the point of the neutral grip.
Hatfield Squat: Set the bar on your back and hold light supports or a rack in front of you with both hands for balance. Squat down keeping your torso upright, using the supports only to stay steady rather than to pull yourself up. Leaning on the supports to help lift the weight turns this into an assisted squat.
Heel-Elevated Squat: Stand with your heels raised on a wedge or plates, bar across your upper back. Squat down keeping your torso more upright than a flat-footed squat, then drive back up. Letting the knees stay back instead of tracking forward over the toes undoes the point of the heel lift.
Helms Row: Set an incline bench and lie face down with a dumbbell in each hand hanging below your shoulders. Row the dumbbells up towards your hips, driving the elbows back and slightly out, then lower fully. Rowing straight up towards the chest instead of down towards the hip changes which part of the back does the work.
Hex Bar Shrug: Stand inside the hex bar holding the handles at your sides. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause briefly, then lower them fully. Bending the knees to help heave the weight up turns the shrug into a partial deadlift.
Incline Barbell Bench Press: Lie back on an inclined bench with the bar over your upper chest. Lower the bar to your upper chest with elbows tucked slightly, then press it back up over your shoulders. Letting the bar drift towards your neck as it comes down puts unwanted strain on the shoulder.
Incline Dumbbell Curl: Sit back on an inclined bench with your arms hanging straight down, holding a dumbbell in each hand. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders without letting your elbows travel forward, then lower fully. The incline stretches the muscle at the bottom, so avoid cutting the lowering phase short.
Incline Dumbbell Fly: Lie on an inclined bench holding dumbbells above your chest with a slight bend in the elbows. Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch, then bring them back together above your chest. Bending the elbows more as the set gets hard turns the fly into a press.
Incline Dumbbell Press: Lie back on an inclined bench holding dumbbells at your upper chest, palms facing your feet. Press the dumbbells up and slightly together, then lower them back to the sides of your upper chest. Setting the bench too steep shifts most of the work onto the front shoulders.
Incline Hammer Curl: Sit back on an inclined bench with your arms hanging straight down, holding dumbbells with palms facing each other. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then lower them fully under control. Letting the elbows drift forward off the line of the torso reduces the stretch this position is meant to give.
Incline Shrug: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding dumbbells hanging straight below your shoulders. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause, then lower them fully. Rowing the elbows back instead of shrugging straight up turns this into a different exercise.
Jefferson Curl: Stand on a raised platform holding a light dumbbell or plate with both hands, feet close together. Round your spine forward from the top down, one vertebra at a time, lowering the weight towards your feet, then reverse the curl to stand back up. Using more than a light load defeats the slow, controlled purpose of the movement.
Jefferson Squat: Straddle the bar with one foot forward and one back, gripping it between your legs. Squat straight down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through both feet evenly. Letting more weight shift onto the front leg turns it into an uneven, awkward lift.
JM Press: Lie on a bench holding the bar with a shoulder-width grip over your chest. Lower the bar towards your neck and chest by bending the elbows, keeping them tucked, then press back up along the same path. Losing the tucked elbow position partway through turns the press into a normal bench press.
Keg Carry: Hug a keg or heavy sandbag tightly against your chest and stand up straight before you start moving. Walk forward with short, controlled steps, keeping your torso upright and the load pulled in close. Letting the load drift away from your chest strains the lower back.
Kettlebell Clean and Press: Start with the kettlebell on the floor between your feet, hike it back then pull it up close to your body into the rack position at your shoulder. From the rack, press the kettlebell overhead, then lower it back to the rack before lowering to the floor. Letting the kettlebell bang hard into the wrist during the clean means the pull path needs to stay closer to the body.
Kettlebell Romanian Deadlift: Stand holding the kettlebell with both hands in front of your thighs. Push your hips back and lower the kettlebell down your legs with a flat back, then drive your hips forward to stand. Bending the knees heavily turns the hinge into a squat.
Kettlebell Shrug: Stand tall holding a kettlebell in each hand or one in both hands at your sides. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause, then lower them fully. Bending the elbows to help the weight up takes tension off the traps.
Kettlebell Snatch: Start with the kettlebell hiked back between your legs, then drive your hips forward to send it upward close to your body. As it rises, punch your hand through so the kettlebell rotates smoothly onto the back of your wrist overhead. Fighting the rotation with a tense wrist causes the kettlebell to bang instead of land softly.
Kettlebell Swing: Stand with the kettlebell in front of you, hinge back to hike it between your legs, then drive your hips forward hard to swing it up to chest height. Let it swing back down between your legs as you hinge again, repeating the rhythm. Squatting the movement instead of hinging at the hips turns it into a completely different exercise.
Kickstand Hip Thrust: Sit against a bench with the bar over your hips, most of your weight on one flat foot and the other foot back on its toes for light support. Drive through the flat heel to lift your hips, then lower under control. Letting the back foot bear real weight reduces the single-leg emphasis of the exercise.
Kneeling Dumbbell Press: Kneel upright on both knees holding dumbbells at shoulder height. Press the dumbbells straight overhead without leaning back, then lower them under control. Arching the lower back to help the press up is the usual compensation when the core is not braced.
Kneeling Squat: Kneel on a pad with the bar across your upper back, sitting your hips back towards your heels. Push your hips forward to rise back up to the kneeling start position. This is a smaller range than a standing squat, so trying to add too much depth is the common overreach.
Kroc Row: Rest one knee and hand on a bench, holding a heavy dumbbell in the other hand hanging below your shoulder. Pull the dumbbell up towards your hip with a bit of body English allowed, then lower it under control. Losing all control on the way down defeats the point of using a heavier load.
Landmine Chest Press (Single-Arm): Stand holding the end of the landmine bar at shoulder height with one hand, feet staggered for balance. Press the bar forward and slightly up until your arm is extended, then bring it back to your shoulder. Letting the torso twist to help the press takes the isolation out of the single arm.
Landmine Front Raise: Stand holding the end of the landmine bar with both hands in front of your thighs. Raise the bar in front of you to around shoulder height with straight arms, then lower under control. Using your lower back to heave the bar up is the common shortcut under fatigue.
Landmine Lateral Raise: Stand side-on to the landmine, holding the end of the bar with the arm furthest from it. Raise the bar out to the side to around shoulder height, then lower under control. Letting the torso lean away to help the lift takes tension off the shoulder.
Landmine Press: Stand holding the end of the landmine bar at shoulder height with both hands, feet staggered. Press the bar forward and up until your arms are extended, then bring it back to your shoulder. Leaning too far forward to help the press changes the angle the shoulder is working through.
Landmine Press (Abs): Kneel or stand holding the end of the landmine bar with both hands at chest height, core braced. Press the bar forward and slightly up while resisting any twist or lean in your torso, then bring it back. Letting the hips rotate with the press takes the challenge away from the core.
Landmine Rear Delt Row: Stand over the landmine bar bent forward at the hips, gripping underneath the bar near the collar. Pull the bar up towards your chest, driving your elbows out wide, then lower under control. Standing too upright removes the forward lean this row depends on.
Landmine Romanian Deadlift: Stand over the landmine bar bent forward slightly, holding the end with both hands close to your body. Push your hips back and lower the bar down your legs with a flat back, then drive your hips forward to stand. Letting the bar drift away from your legs pulls the lower back out of a safe position.
Landmine Rotation: Stand holding the end of the landmine bar with both hands at chest height, arms extended. Rotate your torso and hips to swing the bar from one side down towards the floor, then reverse to the other side. Bending the arms to help the swing takes the rotation work away from the core.
Landmine Row: Stand over the landmine bar, hinge forward at the hips, and grip underneath the bar near the collar. Pull the bar up towards your ribs, driving your elbow back, then lower under control. Standing up out of the hinge as you pull turns the row into a shrug.
Landmine Squat: Stand holding the end of the landmine bar with both hands close to your chest. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. Letting the bar drift away from the chest pulls your torso forward.
Landmine Tricep Extension: Kneel facing away from the landmine, holding the end of the bar behind your head with both hands. Extend your arms to press the bar up and forward, then lower it back behind your head under control. Letting the elbows flare outward spreads the load away from the triceps.
Landmine Twist: Stand holding the end of the landmine bar with both hands at chest height, arms extended. Rotate your torso and hips to swing the bar from one side down towards the floor, then reverse to the other side. Bending the arms to help the swing takes the rotation work away from the core.
Lateral Lunge: Stand tall and take a wide step out to one side, sitting your hips back and bending that knee while the other leg stays straight. Push back through the bent leg to return to standing. Letting the bent knee drift inward instead of tracking over the foot puts strain on the knee.
Leaning Lateral Raise: Hold a support with one hand and lean your torso away from it so the raising arm hangs free with a dumbbell. Raise the dumbbell out to the side, letting the lean add extra range, then lower under control. Standing upright removes the extra stretch this leaning position is meant to give.
Lying Rear Delt Row: Lie face down on an inclined bench, arms hanging straight down holding dumbbells. Row the dumbbells up towards your ribs, driving your elbows out and back, then lower fully. Lifting the chest off the pad to help the pull takes the strictness out of the movement.
Lying Tricep Extension: Lie on a bench holding dumbbells above your chest with arms extended. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells towards your head, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back up. Letting the elbows travel backward past your head changes where the tension sits.
Meadows Row: Stand side-on to a landmine bar, hinge forward at the hips, and grip the bar close to the sleeve with one hand. Pull the bar up towards your hip, driving your elbow back, then lower under control. Rotating the torso to help the pull takes the isolation out of the single arm.
Overhead Dumbbell Extension: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell with both hands behind your head, elbows pointing forward. Extend your arms to press the dumbbell overhead, then lower it back behind your head under control. Letting the elbows flare outward spreads the load away from the triceps.
Pause Squat: Set the bar on your back and squat down as you normally would. At the bottom, hold the position without bouncing for a moment, then drive back up. Relaxing the tension during the pause instead of staying braced makes the drive back up much harder.
Pendlay Row: Set up bent over with a flat back and the bar resting on the floor between reps. Pull the bar explosively up to your lower ribs, driving your elbows back, then return it fully to the floor each rep. Letting the hips rise as you pull turns the row into a partial deadlift.
Pin Squat: Set the safety pins in a rack at your target depth and stand under the bar racked just above them. Squat down until the bar touches the pins, pause briefly without resting the weight down, then drive back up. Letting the whole weight settle onto the pins turns this into a different exercise from the pause version.
Pinch Grip Carry: Pinch a pair of weight plates between your fingers and thumb on each side, smooth sides facing out. Stand tall and walk forward with short, controlled steps. Letting your fingers curl the plate against your palm instead of pinching it removes the point of the exercise.
Plank Row: Hold a plank position with your hands on dumbbells, feet set wide for stability. Row one dumbbell up towards your hip while keeping your hips square to the floor, then lower and repeat on the other side. Letting the hips rotate as you row takes the challenge away from the core.
Plate Front Raise: Stand holding a weight plate with both hands in front of your thighs. Raise the plate in front of you to around shoulder height with straight arms, then lower under control. Using your lower back to heave the plate up is the common shortcut under fatigue.
Plate Lateral Raise: Stand holding a weight plate vertically in front of you with both hands. Raise the plate out to shoulder height, keeping it roughly vertical, then lower under control. Letting the plate tip flat changes the leverage and makes the raise easier than intended.
Plate Neck Curl: Lie on a bench with your head hanging off the end, holding a light plate against your forehead with both hands. Tuck your chin towards your chest to curl your head forward, then return to neutral under control. Using more than a very light plate is the common overreach with this small muscle group.
Plate Neck Extension: Lie face down on a bench with your head hanging off the end, a light plate held against the back of your head. Lift your head back to extend your neck, then lower under control to neutral. Jerking the head up quickly instead of moving smoothly is the usual mistake.
Plate Neck Lateral Flexion: Lie on your side on a bench with your head hanging off the end, a light plate held against the side of your head. Lift your head sideways towards your shoulder, then lower back to neutral under control. Using a plate too heavy for this small range is the main thing to avoid.
Plate Pinch: Pinch two weight plates together between your fingers and thumb, smooth sides facing out. Hold the plates steady at your side for the duration rather than moving them. Letting the plates rotate and slip in your grip means you are gripping too loosely to hold position.
Power Clean: Start with the bar over the middle of your feet, hips set and back flat. Pull the bar up explosively, extending through the hips, then drop under it to catch it across your front shoulders in a quarter squat. Catching the bar too high with rounded shoulders instead of racking it properly on the shoulders is the common miss.
Preacher Curl (Barbell): Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting on the pad, holding the bar with an underhand grip. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it until your arms are almost straight. Lifting your upper arms off the pad to finish the rep takes the strictness out of the movement.
Preacher Curl (Dumbbell): Sit at the preacher bench with one upper arm resting on the pad, holding a dumbbell. Curl the dumbbell up towards your shoulder, then lower it until your arm is almost straight. Lifting the upper arm off the pad to finish the rep takes the strictness out of the movement.
Preacher Curl (EZ Bar): Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting on the pad and the angled bar held with an underhand grip. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it until your arms are almost straight. Lifting your upper arms off the pad to finish the rep takes the strictness out of the movement.
Prone Incline Curl: Lie face down on an inclined bench with your arms hanging straight down, holding dumbbells. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders without letting the elbows travel forward, then lower fully. This position removes any swing, so relying on momentum simply will not work here.
Prone Incline T-Raise: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding light dumbbells hanging straight below you. Raise your arms straight out to the sides to form a T shape, then lower under control. Bending the elbows to make the raise easier reduces the work on the rear shoulder.
Prone Incline Y-Raise: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding light dumbbells hanging straight below you. Raise your arms up and out to form a Y shape above your head, then lower under control. Using too much weight makes it impossible to keep the arms in the Y position throughout.
Push Press: Stand with the bar racked on your front shoulders, feet hip-width apart. Dip slightly at the knees, then drive up through your legs to help press the bar overhead, finishing with arms locked out. Pressing purely with the arms without using the leg drive turns this back into a strict press.
Rack Pull: Set the bar on pins at around knee height and stand close to it with a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the bar close to your legs throughout. Starting with the hips too low for this raised bar height turns the pull into an awkward half squat.
Rack Pull (Traps): Set the bar on pins at around knee height and stand close to it with a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, then finish each rep with a strong shrug at the top. Skipping the shrug at lockout misses the point of this trap-focused version.
Renegade Row: Hold a plank position with your hands on dumbbells, feet set wide for stability. Row one dumbbell up towards your hip while keeping your hips square to the floor, then lower and repeat on the other side. Letting the hips rotate as you row takes the challenge away from the core.
Reverse Curl: Stand holding a bar with an overhand grip, elbows at your sides. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders keeping your wrists firm, then lower under control. Letting the wrists bend or flick during the curl takes tension away from the forearms.
Reverse Lunge: Stand tall and step one leg backward, lowering your back knee towards the floor while your front shin stays close to vertical. Push through the front foot to return to standing. Letting the front knee travel far past the toes puts unnecessary strain on the joint.
Reverse Lunge (Glute Focus): Stand tall and step one leg backward, sitting your hips down and back as you lower rather than straight down. Drive through the front heel to return to standing, keeping the torso slightly forward. Standing up onto the toes of the front foot takes the tension off the glute.
Reverse Wrist Curl: Sit and rest your forearms on your thighs, palms down, holding a bar or dumbbells. Lift your knuckles up as far as comfortable, then lower until your wrists are fully bent the other way. Using the whole forearm to swing the weight reduces the isolation on the wrist.
Reverse-Grip Bench Press: Lie on the bench and take an underhand grip on the bar, hands shoulder-width apart. Lower the bar to your upper chest keeping your elbows tucked, then press it back up. Letting the elbows flare wide on this grip puts more strain on the shoulders than the standard grip.
Romanian Deadlift: Stand holding the bar at your thighs with a flat back and soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower the bar down your legs until you feel a stretch in the hamstrings, then drive your hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back as the bar passes the knee is the usual fault.
Romanian Deadlift (Barbell): Stand holding the bar at your thighs with a flat back and soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower the bar down your legs until you feel a stretch in the hamstrings, then drive your hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back as the bar passes the knee is the usual fault.
Romanian Deadlift (Dumbbell): Stand holding dumbbells at your thighs with a flat back and soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back and lower the dumbbells down your legs until you feel a stretch in the hamstrings, then drive your hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back as the weight passes the knee is the usual fault.
Romanian Deadlift (Glute): Stand holding the bar at your thighs with a flat back and soft bend in the knees. Push your hips back further than a standard hinge and lower the bar down your legs, then squeeze your glutes hard to drive forward and stand. Hinging with too little hip push turns this back into a hamstring-focused version.
Safety Bar Squat: Set the padded bar across your shoulders, gripping the front handles, and stand tall. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. The forward handles pull your torso forward more than a straight bar, so bracing your core hard matters more here.
Seal Row: Lie face down on a raised bench with the bar or dumbbells hanging below you, feet off the floor. Row the weight up towards your torso, driving your elbows back, then lower fully. Kicking the legs to help the pull is a sign the weight is too heavy for strict control.
Seated Calf Raise (Barbell): Sit with the balls of your feet on a raised block and a padded bar resting across your knees. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, then lower your heels for a full stretch. Bouncing at the bottom instead of pausing takes the tension off the calf.
Seated Dumbbell Calf Raise: Sit with the balls of your feet on a raised block and dumbbells resting on your knees. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, then lower your heels for a full stretch. Bouncing at the bottom instead of pausing takes the tension off the calf.
Seated Dumbbell Curl: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with your arms hanging at your sides. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then lower them under control. Leaning back against the bench to swing the weight up removes the strictness sitting is meant to add.
Seated Dumbbell Press: Sit on a bench holding dumbbells at shoulder height with your back supported. Press the dumbbells straight up until your arms are extended, then lower them back to shoulder height. Arching away from the back support to help the press changes the angle of the lift.
Seated Lateral Raise: Sit on a bench holding dumbbells at your sides with a slight bend in the elbows. Raise your arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height, then lower under control. Sitting removes the ability to lean back and cheat, so using too much weight shows up quickly.
Seated Twist (Plate): Sit on the floor or a bench with your knees bent, holding a weight plate with both hands in front of your chest. Rotate your torso to tap the plate down on one side, then rotate through to the other side. Moving quickly with momentum instead of a controlled rotation reduces the work on the obliques.
Single-Arm Dumbbell Press: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell at shoulder height on one side, keeping the torso braced. Press the dumbbell straight overhead without leaning to the opposite side, then lower it back to shoulder height. Letting the torso tip away from the working arm is the usual compensation as the weight gets heavy.
Single-Arm Dumbbell Shrug: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side. Lift that shoulder straight up towards your ear, pause, then lower it fully. Leaning the torso towards the working side to help the lift takes the isolation out of the shrug.
Single-Arm Farmer Carry: Stand holding a heavy dumbbell in one hand, standing up tall with the other side braced against leaning. Walk forward with short, controlled steps, resisting the pull of the weight to one side. Letting the torso tip towards the loaded side is the usual sign the core has stopped bracing.
Single-Arm Landmine Row: Stand over the landmine bar, hinge forward at the hips, and grip underneath the bar near the collar with one hand. Pull the bar up towards your ribs, driving your elbow back, then lower under control. Rotating the torso to help the pull takes the isolation out of the single arm.
Single-Leg Calf Raise (Dumbbell): Stand on one foot with the ball of that foot on a raised edge, holding a dumbbell in the same-side hand. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, then lower your heel for a full stretch. Letting the other foot take weight through the floor reduces the load on the working calf.
Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift: Stand on one leg holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand, with a soft bend in the standing knee. Hinge forward at the hip, letting your free leg rise behind you for balance, until your torso is close to horizontal. Rounding the lower back to reach further down is the usual mistake as balance wobbles.
Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift (DB): Stand on one leg holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand, with a soft bend in the standing knee. Hinge forward at the hip, letting your free leg rise behind you for balance, until your torso is close to horizontal. Rounding the lower back to reach further down is the usual mistake as balance wobbles.
Snatch Grip Deadlift: Stand with a very wide grip on the bar, hips set lower than a conventional deadlift and back flat. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout. Letting the wider grip pull your shoulders forward rounds the upper back under load.
Snatch Grip Shrug: Stand tall holding the bar with a very wide grip in front of your thighs. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause briefly, then lower them fully. Bending the elbows to help the weight up takes tension off the traps.
Spider Curl: Lie face down on an inclined bench with your arms hanging straight down over the top, holding the bar. Curl the bar up towards your forehead, then lower it fully under control. This position removes any swing, so relying on momentum simply will not work here.
Split Squat: Stand with one foot forward and one back in a staggered stance, bar across your upper back. Lower your back knee towards the floor by bending both legs, then push back up through the front foot. Letting the front knee cave inward under fatigue is the main thing to watch.
SSB Squat: Set the padded bar across your shoulders, gripping the front handles, and stand tall. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. The forward handles pull your torso forward more than a straight bar, so bracing your core hard matters more here.
Standing Calf Raise (Barbell): Stand with the bar across your upper back and the balls of your feet on a raised edge. Rise up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, then lower your heels below the edge for a full stretch. Bouncing at the bottom instead of pausing takes the tension off the calf.
Step-Up (Barbell): Stand facing a box or bench with the bar across your upper back. Step one foot fully onto the box and drive through it to stand tall on top, then step back down under control. Pushing off the trailing foot instead of the working leg takes the effort away from the leg on the box.
Step-Up (Dumbbell): Stand facing a box or bench holding dumbbells at your sides. Step one foot fully onto the box and drive through it to stand tall on top, then step back down under control. Pushing off the trailing foot instead of the working leg takes the effort away from the leg on the box.
Step-Up (Glute Focus): Stand facing a taller box holding dumbbells, and step up leading with a slight forward lean from the hips. Drive through the heel of the leading foot to stand tall on top, then step back down under control. Standing too upright shifts the emphasis away from the glute and onto the quad.
Step-Up (Weighted): Stand facing a box or bench holding dumbbells at your sides. Step one foot fully onto the box and drive through it to stand tall on top, then step back down under control. Pushing off the trailing foot instead of the working leg takes the effort away from the leg on the box.
Stiff-Leg Deadlift: Stand holding the bar at your thighs with your knees only slightly bent, more locked than a Romanian deadlift. Push your hips back and lower the bar down your legs with a flat back, then drive your hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back to reach lower is the usual fault as the hamstrings run out of range.
Stiff-Leg Deadlift (Dumbbell): Stand holding dumbbells at your thighs with your knees only slightly bent, more locked than a Romanian deadlift. Push your hips back and lower the weights down your legs with a flat back, then drive your hips forward to stand. Rounding the lower back to reach lower is the usual fault as the hamstrings run out of range.
Stiff-Leg Deadlift (Single-Leg): Stand on one leg holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand, knee only slightly bent. Hinge forward at the hip, letting your free leg rise behind you for balance, until you feel a stretch in the hamstring. Rounding the lower back to reach further down is the usual mistake as balance wobbles.
Suitcase Carry: Stand holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side, as if carrying a suitcase, torso upright. Walk forward with short, controlled steps, resisting the pull of the weight to one side. Letting the torso lean towards the loaded side is the usual sign the core has stopped bracing.
Sumo Deadlift: Stand with a wide stance, toes turned out, gripping the bar inside your knees with a flat back. Push your knees out in the direction of your toes and drive through the floor to stand tall. Letting the hips shoot up faster than the chest turns the pull into a stiff-legged lift.
Sumo Deadlift (Glute Focus): Stand with a wide stance, toes turned out, gripping the bar inside your knees with a flat back. Drive through the floor and squeeze the glutes hard as you finish tall, pushing the hips through rather than just standing up. Skipping the final glute squeeze reduces the emphasis this version is built for.
Sumo Deadlift (Wide Stance): Stand with a wide stance, toes turned out, gripping the bar inside your knees with a flat back. Push your knees out in the direction of your toes and drive through the floor to stand tall. Letting the hips shoot up faster than the chest turns the pull into a stiff-legged lift.
Sumo Squat: Stand with a wide stance and toes turned out, bar across your upper back or held at your chest. Squat straight down, pushing your knees out over your toes, then drive back up. Letting the knees collapse inward is the most common breakdown with a wide stance.
Sumo Squat (Adductor Focus): Stand with a wide stance and toes turned out further than a standard sumo squat, holding a dumbbell at your chest. Squat down, actively pushing your knees out over your toes, then drive back up. Letting the knees track less than the toes reduces the inner-thigh emphasis this stance is meant to add.
Sumo Squat (Glute Focus): Stand with a wide stance and toes turned out, holding a dumbbell at your chest. Squat down and drive up through your heels, squeezing the glutes hard at the top of each rep. Rising onto the toes at the top shifts the finish away from the glutes.
Svend Press: Stand holding a weight plate pressed flat between both palms at chest height, squeezing it throughout. Press the plate straight out in front of you without letting go of the squeeze, then bring it back to your chest. Letting the squeeze on the plate ease off removes the whole point of the exercise.
T-Bar Row: Straddle the bar or machine, hinge forward at the hips with a flat back, and grip the handles. Pull the weight up towards your torso, driving your elbows back, then lower it fully under control. Standing up out of the hinge as you pull turns the row into a shrug.
Tate Press: Lie on a bench holding dumbbells above your chest with palms facing your feet. Bend your elbows out to the sides to lower the dumbbells towards your chest, then extend back up. Letting the elbows drop back towards your head instead of out to the sides turns it into a different tricep exercise.
Thick Bar Curl: Stand holding a bar fitted with a thick grip or wrapped padding, elbows at your sides. Curl the bar up towards your shoulders, then lower it under control, keeping a firm grip throughout. Letting the grip loosen partway through the set is the main reason this version feels harder.
Trap Bar Deadlift: Stand inside the hex-shaped bar with your feet under the handles and a flat back. Drive through the floor to stand tall, keeping the weight close to your body throughout. Letting the hips rise faster than the chest turns the pull into a stiff-legged lift.
Trap Bar Deadlift (Hamstring): Stand inside the hex-shaped bar with your feet under the handles and a flat back, hips set slightly lower than usual. Push your hips back more than forward as you drive up, feeling the stretch through the hamstrings. Letting the knees do most of the work turns this back into a quad-dominant pull.
Trap Bar Shrug: Stand inside the hex bar holding the handles at your sides. Lift your shoulders straight up towards your ears, pause briefly, then lower them fully. Bending the knees to help heave the weight up turns the shrug into a partial deadlift.
Tricep Kickback: Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back, upper arm held close to your side and parallel to the floor, elbow bent. Extend your arm straight back until it is fully locked out, then bend it back to the start. Letting the upper arm drop down or swing forward takes the isolation out of the triceps.
Turkish Get-Up: Lie on your back holding a kettlebell pressed straight up over one shoulder, opposite knee bent. Work through the sequence of postures, from elbow to hand to standing, keeping your eyes on the kettlebell throughout, then reverse the whole sequence back down. Letting your eyes drop off the kettlebell partway through is the usual reason the weight starts to wobble.
Upright Row: Stand holding a bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip in front of your thighs. Pull the bar straight up towards your collarbone, leading with your elbows out to the sides, then lower with control. Pulling the bar too high above the collarbone brings unwanted strain into the shoulder joint.
W-Raise: Stand or lie face down holding light dumbbells hanging below you. Raise your arms out and up into a W shape, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top, then lower under control. Using too much weight to hold the W shape turns the movement into a shrug.
Waiter Curl: Stand holding a dumbbell vertically under the top plate with both hands, as if balancing a tray. Curl the dumbbell up towards your shoulders keeping it upright, then lower under control. Letting the dumbbell tip sideways shows the grip and wrist position have broken down.
Walking Lunge: Stand tall holding dumbbells at your sides and step forward into a lunge, then push off the back foot to bring it through into the next lunge. Keep your front shin close to vertical on each step as you travel forward. Letting the front knee travel far past the toes puts unnecessary strain on the joint.
Walking Lunge (Glute Focus): Stand tall holding dumbbells and step forward into a lunge with a slight forward lean, then push through the front heel to bring the back foot through into the next step. Driving through the heel rather than the toes keeps the emphasis on the glute. Standing too upright on each step shifts the work back onto the quads.
Wall Ball Squat: Hold a weighted ball at your chest and squat down between your knees, keeping your torso upright. Drive back up through the middle of your foot to standing. Letting the ball drift away from the chest pulls your torso forward and shortens your depth.
Weighted Frog Pump: Lie on your back with the soles of your feet together and knees dropped out to the sides, a dumbbell resting on your hips. Drive your hips up towards the ceiling, squeezing your glutes hard at the top, then lower under control. Letting the knees drift together instead of staying wide takes the focus off the glutes.
Weighted Plank (Plate on Back): Get into a forearm plank position with a weight plate placed flat across your upper back. Hold your body in a straight line from head to heels without letting your hips sag or pike up. Letting the hips sag under the extra load is the first sign the position is breaking down.
Weighted Russian Twist (Medicine Ball): Sit with your knees bent and feet either on the floor or lifted, leaning back slightly, holding the ball at your chest. Rotate your torso to tap the ball down on one side, then rotate through to the other side. Moving quickly with momentum instead of a controlled rotation reduces the work on the obliques.
Weighted Sit-Up: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet anchored, holding a weight plate against your chest. Curl your torso up until you are sitting upright, then lower back down under control. Yanking the head and neck forward to start the movement takes the work away from the abs.
Wide-Stance Goblet Squat (Adductor Bias): Hold a dumbbell vertically against your chest and stand with a wide stance, toes turned out further than a standard goblet squat. Squat down, pushing your knees out in line with your toes, then drive back up. Letting the knees track less than the toes reduces the inner-thigh emphasis this stance is meant to add.
Windmill: Stand with a kettlebell pressed overhead in one hand, feet turned slightly away from that side. Hinge sideways at the hips, sliding your free hand down the inside of your leg while keeping your eyes on the raised kettlebell, then reverse to stand. Letting the pressed arm drift forward instead of staying stacked over the shoulder puts it at an awkward angle.
Wrist Roller: Hold the roller device out in front of you at shoulder height with both hands, a weight hanging from the cord. Roll the handle forward with your wrists to wind the cord up, then roll it back down under control. Dropping your arms to shoulder level or lower halfway through takes tension off the forearms.
YTW: Lie face down on an inclined bench holding light dumbbells hanging below you. Raise your arms to form a Y, then a T, then a W shape in sequence, lowering fully between each, keeping the weight light throughout. Using too much weight for this drill makes it impossible to hold each shape with good form.
Z-Press: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you, holding the bar at shoulder height. Press the bar straight overhead without leaning back for help, then lower it back to shoulder height. Leaning the torso backward to assist the press is the usual compensation this seated position is meant to remove.
Zercher Squat: Hold the bar in the crooks of your elbows against your torso, standing with feet shoulder-width apart. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up through the middle of your foot. Letting the bar roll down towards your wrists instead of staying in the elbow crease makes the hold uncomfortable and unstable.
Zercher Sumo Squat (Adductor Focus): Hold the bar in the crooks of your elbows against your torso, standing with a wide stance and toes turned out. Squat down, pushing your knees out over your toes, then drive back up. Letting the knees track less than the toes reduces the inner-thigh emphasis this stance is meant to add.
Zottman Curl: Stand holding dumbbells with palms facing up. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then rotate your palms to face down before lowering them under control. Forgetting to rotate before lowering turns this back into a normal curl and misses the point of the exercise.
Zottman Preacher Curl: Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting on the pad, holding dumbbells with palms facing up. Curl the weights up towards your shoulders, then rotate your palms to face down before lowering under control. Forgetting to rotate before lowering turns this back into a normal preacher curl.
